newsitem.title: LAOS: Laos says economic growth, hydropower top goals.
newsitem.headline: Laos says economic growth, hydropower top goals.

text.p: The Lao government this week wrapped up three days of discussion over a controversial $1.5 billion dam with a clear message -- it is determined to push forward with the project and other hydropower ventures.

"Hydropower is the priority sector in the Lao (government's) programme of socio-economic development. We strongly believe that hydropower could play an important role in alleviating poverty," Vice Minister of Industry and Handicrafts Khammone Phonekeo said.
The discussion was the second time Laos has publicly debated the fate of the Nam Theun 2 (NT2) dam, providing an unusual glimpse into the inner workings of this small communist nation.
Lao officials indicated they put economic development above most other concerns, including environmental and social considerations.
With half of their population living in poverty, they stressed, helping people survive must take precendence.

"For some people, the NT2 might not be important, especially if they haven't experienced poverty. But if we aren't going to exploit our natural resources, then what are we going to do?" said Deputy Director for Electricity, Somboun Manolom.

"Lao people don't want to wear torn clothes, play the flute and have our picture taken by tourists and say 'This is Laos.' We don't want to be in that position any more," he told the 120 officials, consultants and observers at the meeting.
Analysts said Laos had pinned its hopes on harnessing its rivers, which are thought to represent a total of 23,000 MW in exploitable hydropower.
"The message is, 'we have a lot of water and let's make use of it'," said Engelbertus Oud, project manager of a study of alternatives to the NT2 presented at the meeting.
"We in the West focus entirely on the environment and relatively little on people and here it is the other way around," he told Reuters in an interview.
Phonekeo said hydropower made good economic sense.

"We have the market next door (in Thailand). We have financial support there, and we have a significant number of investors who want to invest in this sector," he said, asserting that hydropower was environmentally and socially sound.
David Iverach, director of the Nam Theun 2 Electricity Consortium (NTEC) that is developing the project, agreed and said the dam "will be a model for Asia."

But some international aid agencies question the toll on Laos' ethnic peoples and forests. By flooding 450 sq kms (170 sq miles) to form a reservoir, the NT2 would displace 1,000 families and put pressure on an adjacent conservation area, they said.

The verdict on those issues will be key to the future of the NT2, which could supply between 681 megawatts and 900 megawatts of power for sale to Thailand as part of Laos' commitment to provide 3,000 megawatts of electricity to its neighbour by 2006.

The government has asked the World Bank to provide $100 million in partial loan guarantees, but the Bank wants three studies into the dam's impact and more public hearings before it makes its decision. The studies are expected to be completed mid-year and more hearings are slated for June.

NTEC, which includes Transfield Corp, Electricite de France, Italian-Thai Development, Thailand's Jasmine International and Phatra Thanakit, said it would pull out if it did not get the World Bank guarantees.
"I don't see any reason why the World Bank will drop out now," Phonekeo said, calling the NT2 a "model of development."
